extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical guidance for composing tragic (and epic) poetry—focusing on plot construction, character, recognition, diction, and dramatic effects to produce pity and fear. Includes rules about scale, metre, chorus, and techniques of composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single complete action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot should have a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poem or play should resemble a living organism in unity; avoid treating a vast subject (e.g., whole war) as a single drama. Select a portion of the larger story and, if using episodes, make them relevant and subordinate to the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper scale and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; keep the scale appropriate to the medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy must be more limited than epic; do not use multiplicity of plots or attempt to dramatize the whole epic narrative. Epic allows greater enlargement and simultaneous lines of action; tragedy should avoid over-complication by length or multiple plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and Unravelling (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication (from the beginning to the turning-point) and Unravelling/Denouement (from the change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the turning-point clearly; ensure incidents extraneous to the action are not conflated with the action proper unless they serve the Complication. Both knot-tying (complication) and unravelling must be well-managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Reversal (peripeteia) and Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex tragedy depends entirely on Reversal of the Situation and Recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ reversal and recognition as central mechanisms to generate dramatic change; combine these with other poetic elements where possible for maximal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy and combination of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of tragedy: Complex (reversal + recognition), Pathetic (motive is passion), Ethical (motives are ethical), and Simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, endeavor to combine the greatest number and the most important poetic elements; do not restrict the work to a single weak element if a richer combination is attainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality: necessity and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should aim at the necessary or the probable in both plot and portraiture; events should follow by necessity or probable sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrational actions within the scope of the drama; if irrational elements cannot be excluded they should lie outside the action proper (e.g., as antecedent or subsequent events). Ensure unravelling and complication arise out of the plot itself, not from arbitrary invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance and limited use of Deus ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Deus ex Machina' must be employed only for events external to the drama—antecedent or subsequent events which lie beyond human knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use divine contrivance to resolve or create events within the action proper; doing so weakens artistic integrity (examples: Medea, Return of the Greeks in the Iliad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents that arouse pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing pity and fear usually occur between persons who are friends, near, dear, or related to one another rather than between indifferent parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tragic incidents where kinship or intimate relations are involved (brother killing brother, son and father, mother and son, etc.). Such ties intensify pity and fear beyond mere suffering in strangers or enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred mode of tragic deed (ignorant commission + later discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of possible modes, the best is where the deed is perpetrated in ignorance and the tie of kinship or friendship is discovered afterwards; this produces the most startling and tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking: (best) deed committed in ignorance with later discovery; (better) deed perpetrated knowingly; (worse) about to act with knowledge and then not act (shocking but not tragic). Use the ignorance/discovery form when possible to maximize tragic impact (examples: Oedipus, Alcmaeon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: goodness, propriety, truth-to-life, consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at: (1) it must be good; (2) it must have propriety (appropriate traits for the class/gender/status); (3) it must be true to life; (4) it must be consistent (even consistently inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness is relative to class (a woman or slave may be 'good' within their class). Avoid motiveless degradation, indecorous behavior, and characters who behave without credible motive. If a character is inconsistent, portray that inconsistency consistently so it reads as a coherent type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character actions should arise from character (necessity/probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of a given character should speak or act in a given way by the rule either of necessity or of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure plot unravelling and complication flow from character-driven causes rather than arbitrary contrivance. The action must grow out of the character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors and be an integral part of the whole, sharing in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral songs that are mere interludes unrelated to the subject of the piece (a later fault of some tragedians); design the Chorus to participate meaningfully in the drama as in Sophocles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition methods and their artistic ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions vary: by signs/tokens, by turn of incident, invented by poet, by memory, by reasoning, and composite kinds; the best are recognitions arising naturally from the incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Least artistic: recognition by signs/tokens or formal proofs used merely for proof. Avoid poetically invented recognitions (characters saying what the poet wants rather than what plot requires). Prefer recognitions that spring from incident (e.g., Oedipus) or reasoning/memory where natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial or poet-invented recognitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at will by the poet (where a character unnaturally announces identity or recognition) are lacking in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not have characters reveal identity or recognition for the sake of plot convenience when the plot does not naturally require it (examples: Orestes revealing himself in some plays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spectacle sparingly; prefer inner structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means, but the better and superior method is to produce them from the inner structure of the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence on spectacle produces a sense of the monstrous rather than the terrible; strive to make the tale thrilling to the ear alone (i.e., effective in narrative without visual aids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition process: outline then episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether taking a story ready-made or constructing it, first sketch the general outline and then fill in episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure episodes are relevant to the action (e.g., in Orestes the madness and purificatory rite are relevant); use episodes to extend an epic but keep episodes in drama short and pertinent to the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the scene vividly and check for stage-consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes so that, seeing everything vividly, he will avoid inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize staging, gestures, and physical relations to prevent errors that offend spectators (example: oversight in Carcinus where Amphiaraus' movement was stage-inconsistent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture and delivery support emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Work out the play with appropriate gestures; those who feel emotion are most convincing by natural sympathy and corresponding movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gesture and delivery to make emotion convincing (agitated persons storm, angry persons rage); delivery falls under the art of performance but the poet should plan for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Thought: rhetorical aims and dramatic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (proof, refutation, excitation of feelings, suggestion of importance) is part of dramatic speech; incidents should speak for themselves while speech produces effects by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic incidents must be treated from same points of view as speeches to evoke pity, fear, and probability. Speech must be crafted to produce intended effects; avoid revealing Thought apart from what a character would naturally say.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of utterance (delivery) belong to performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes of utterance (command, prayer, statement, threat, question, answer, etc.) belong to the art of Delivery rather than the poet's craft alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the poet need not be faulted for not specifying every delivery mode, awareness of these distinctions informs effective speech-writing and collaboration with performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style uses only current/proper words but is mean; a loftier diction uses unusual words, metaphors, and ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance current words (for clarity) with strange/rare words, metaphor, and ornamental devices (for distinction). Use lengthening, contraction, and alteration sparingly and with propriety. Excessive use of rare words or metaphors produces riddles or jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor and propriety of word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: To have a command of metaphor is the greatest thing by far; using metaphor appropriately is a mark of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different genres demand different word types: compound words suit Dithyrambs, rare words heroic poetry, metaphors iambic, while iambic verse benefits from words found in prose. Use metaphors with an eye for resemblances and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses of speech (lengthening, contraction, alteration) with moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words give distinction but must be employed with moderation and propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial conformity with usage gives perspicuity; obtrusive or grotesque manipulation of forms (e.g., excessive lengthening) becomes ludicrous. Critics who censure these licenses may err if employed judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre for narrative scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry requires the heroic measure (stateliest and most massive); mixing metres or using unsuitable metre for large-scale narrative is incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroic metre admits rare words and metaphors and suits the narrative form. Iambic and trochaic tetrameter are stirring and suit action and dance respectively. Do not mix different metres in large-scale poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's personal intrusion should be minimal
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, for it is not this that makes him an imitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize authorial commentary; allow the imitation and characters to present the action and Thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of language components and metrical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of language parts (letter, syllable, connecting word, noun, verb, inflexion, sentence) and sound qualities (vowel, semi-vowel, mute; long/short; aspirated/smooth) informs diction and metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding phonetics, syllable structure and inflexion helps in metrical composition and diction choices. While detailed metrical inquiry belongs to metrical science, the poet should be informed of these elements.
